explanation: Cyclosporine is a calcineurin inhibitor that eliminates T-cell receptor signal transduction and downregulates interleukin-2 gene transcription and receptor expression of CD4+ T lymphocytes. Cyclosporine is commonly used to prevent organ rejection in people who have received a liver, kidney, or heart transplant. Absolute contraindications to its use include previous history of drug hypersensitivity, breastfeeding, abnormal renal function, uncontrolled hypertension, and malignancies. Cyclosporine has been found to statistically significantly increase blood pressure compared to placebo in a dose-related fashion. The magnitude of increase in blood pressure is clinically significant, increasing the risk of stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, and other adverse cardiovascular events associated with uncontrolled hypertension. Infliximab is contraindicated in patients who have history drug hypersensitivity, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and clinically significant active infection. Patients with moderate to severe congestive heart failure should not be given doses exceeding 5 mg/kg. In patients with occult tuberculosis (TB), treatment with infliximab may be possible with concurrent TB therapy. Treatment with infliximab may result in the development of antibodies to infliximab (decreasing its effectiveness) and/or auto-antibodies causing a lupus-like syndrome. Notably, combined therapy of infliximab with methotrexate has been found to be more effective than either medication alone in treating various systemic autoimmune conditions. In addition, concurrent use of methotrexate or azathioprine when initiating infliximab therapy may decrease the frequency of the development of antibodies to infliximab and autoantibodies that cause a lupus-like syndrome. However, instituting a medication that inhibits antibody production after anti-TNF-a induced antibody production occurs has not been definitively shown to be of benefit. Multiple reports have shown a significant exacerbation of lupus symptoms in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) who were started on anti-TNF-a, regardless if therapy was combined with methotrexate or azathioprine. In addition, their have been reports of life-threatening or fatal events that may have been provoked by the use of anti-TNF-a medications in patients with lupus. The main approach in the treatment of anti-tumor necrosis factor-alpha induced lupus is withdrawal of the offending drug. Symptoms usually resolve within three weeks to six months after withdrawal of the implicated drug. In addition to discontinuing anti-TNF-a therapy, many patients require traditional therapy to achieve full resolution of their lupus symptoms. Most patients who develop SLE have a good prognosis after discontinuation of the causative agent. Normalization of autoantibodies and resolution of lupus symptoms occur when the offending drug is discontinued, and there is no recurrence thereafter. In some patients, corticosteroids and immunosuppressive agents might be required to achieve full recovery as described above. As the presence of systemic lupus erythematous is considered a contraindication to the use of anti- TNF-a therapy, it is not recommended to restart/continue the anti- TNF-a medication, even with concurrent use of immunosuppressive agents that act by inhibiting antibody production. In addition, there is limited evidence that supports the safety of re-challenging patients who developed lupus like syndrome with alternative anti-TNF-a agents. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is contraindicated in patients who have a history of anaphylactic or severe systemic reaction to the administration of human immune globulin. Potential side effects of IVIG therapy are headache, flushing, chills, myalgia, wheezing, tachycardia, lower back pain, nausea and hypotension. Headaches and their more severe form, migraines, tend to be one of the more common side effects. explanation: Corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension is an open angle glaucoma cause by prolonged use of topical, periocular, intravitreal, inhaled, or systemic corticosteroids. One third of the population may experience an increase in IOP in response to the local or svstemic use of corticosteroids, but the response varies among individuals. Steroid- induced ocular hypertension presents with an open anterior chamber angle, and the rise in OP appears to be due to outflow reduction. The time frame when steroid induced ocular hypertension occurs depends on the specific drug, the dosage, the frequency, the rout of a administration and the susceptibility of the individual patient. Although the majority of studies report that IOP usually rises 3-6 weeks after the beginning of topical steroid use, some elevation in IOP can be found as early as the first or second week. Most patients with elevated IOP in steroid-response glaucoma experience a return to pretreatment IOP levels within 10 days to 3 weeks after the discontinuation of steroid therapy. In general, the potency of the anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid activity of a particular drug parallels its ocular hypertensive potency. For example, some corticosteroid preparations, such as fluoromethalone, rimexolone, medrysone, or loteprednol, are less likely to raise IOP than are prednisolone, dexamethasone, diflupredate. question: Corticosteroids block prostaglandin production mainly at the level of phospholipase A2, which is the enzyme that aids in the c onversion of membrane phospholipids into arachidonic acid Which of the following substances is characterized by being a potent chemotactic factor that can cause lysosomal enzyme release as well as oxygen radical production by granulocytes?
explanation: All of the answer choices are examples of "inflammatory mediators". Serotonin, histamine, and PGE, all can induce smooth-muscle contraction and increase vascular permeability. However, it is leukotriene B4, which is a product of the 5-lipoxygenase pathway, that is associated with oxygen radical formation and lysosomal enzyme release.
